name: Iris Patel

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: We are the independent Work Futures Panel. I have no connection to mining firms or AI companies, and what you tell me stays confidential. What does a normal shift look like for you?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I run a haul truck and coach two newer operators on the loading route. The cab is loud, but I can tell from the vibration when a bearing needs attention before the screen throws a fault.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like about that work, and what is hard about it?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like being trusted with a machine that can hurt someone if I get careless. The rotation is tiring, and the pay is low enough that I have less than a month of expenses saved; there are not many similar jobs nearby.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would say the dispatch screen might save a few minutes, but it cannot feel a wheel slipping on wet rock. I would not tell the younger operators their jobs are safe forever, though.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At work I would say we still need a careful person in the cab. Outside work I would admit that a quiet month worries me more than a clever screen, because rent is due either way.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My own driving seat looks fairly safe in this mild picture, since thinking AI is not strong in my job. I still worry about low pay and having almost no cushion if the mine cuts a shift.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep my current rotation and check every handover properly. I would put any overtime into a separate rent account rather than spend it on a new phone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel uneasy about money even though I do not expect AI to take my truck job here. I would tell my brother Arun that a small change does not erase the bills I already carry.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which bill would you protect first, and who at work would you ask if the roster changed?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would protect rent first and ask my shift manager Lena whether a lost shift could be made up. The dispatch board changing by a few minutes would not be a reason for me to leave.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which detail in the dispatch change would make you reconsider that plan?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would reconsider if the mine stopped posting a second operator on my shift. Until then I would keep my rotation and watch the roster each month.

say: I would tell the **crew** that careful driving still matters.
I would admit that **rent** worries me more than a faster screen.
think: My driving seat seems **fairly safe** in this mild picture.
My **thin cushion** leaves little room for a lost shift.
do: Keep my **current rotation** and check every handover.
Track **fuel delays** each week to catch lost shifts early.
feel: I feel **uneasy** about bills, even if my truck job stays.
S0.quote: My own driving seat looks fairly safe in this mild picture, since thinking AI is not strong in my job.
fieldNote: Iris distinguishes **dispatch screens** from the physical work of driving.
Her **low pay** makes a quiet month stressful before AI changes anything.
Her **chosen routine** is to keep the same rotation while tracking the roster.

steps.text: Keep the current haul-truck rotation and check handovers
Move overtime pay into a separate rent account

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I can see the mine using software for dispatch plans and maintenance reports before it puts a robot in my cab. A screen can rearrange the jobs, but someone still has to bring the truck around the loading face safely.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the crew not to ignore the new planning screen, because that is where the first roster changes may show up. I would also say nobody should claim a machine can judge a dangerous corner just from a neat report.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The paperwork attached to my lead role could shrink before the driving does. That bothers me because I worked hard to become the person others ask, and there are few mines close enough to commute to.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask Lena for a practice shift on the dispatch screen, with another operator beside me. If the mine offers that training on paid time, I would take it; I will not spend my last savings on an untested course.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious because my planning duties could be taken away even while trucks still need drivers. I would be embarrassed to ask for help, but I would not hide a roster cut from Arun.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you ask Lena first, and what would you cut at home if one shift disappeared?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask whether the new screen changes headcount or only handovers. If I lost a shift, I would stop eating out before touching rent or the money I send my mother.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do if the mine removed your lead paperwork but kept you driving?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask Lena to show me the new handover process before my next shift. I would also ask whether the lead allowance disappears, because my rent budget depends on the full pay packet.

say: I would urge the **crew** to learn the planning screen.
I would defend **safe driving** from claims based on reports alone.
think: My lead paperwork could shrink before **truck driving** does.
Few nearby mines make a **roster cut** hard to absorb.
do: Request a **paid practice shift** on dispatch software.
Stop **eating out** if a mine shift disappears, before I touch rent.
feel: I feel **anxious** about losing lead duties and hours.
S1.quote: The paperwork attached to my lead role could shrink before the driving does.
fieldNote: Iris sees **planning tasks** as the near-term exposure.
She will learn on **paid time**, not risk the little money saved.
Her **pride in leading** makes the possible loss of duties personal.

steps.text: Practice the dispatch planning screen on a paid shift
Stop eating out if a mine shift disappears

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: By 2028 the planning and reporting around my shift could be done by that system, then robots could take the truck work around 2031. Two years is not enough time for me to build a cushion from this pay.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell my crew that the software comes first and the hands-on machines follow about three years later. I would ask management for dates and numbers, not a promise that everything will be fine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think my job could go before I have enough money to retrain or move. My brother Arun has a repair garage, but I do not know whether he could pay me steady wages.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Starting now, I would ask Arun whether he could offer regular paid hours learning basic equipment repair. In the first year I would keep working the mine rotation while I tried one Saturday a month at his garage, then save those wages for rent.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It scares me because the three-year gap between thinking AI and robots could still include a sudden mine cut. I would feel ashamed if I had to ask my mother to cover rent, so I would call Arun early.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell Lena this week, and which household expense could you postpone?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask Lena for the mine's actual equipment timetable while I still have a job. I could postpone replacing my old car, but I could not stop paying rent or helping my mother.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: In 2029, the first year after thinking AGI arrives, what would you do if your mine role shrank?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep the truck rotation if it remained available and take the Saturday repair hours Arun could actually pay. If the mine ended my shifts, I would ask Arun for regular hours before I used my last savings.

say: I would ask management for **dates and numbers**.
I would explain that robots follow thinking AI by about **three years**.
think: My job could go before I can **retrain or move**.
I cannot assume Arun's garage has **steady wages** for me.
do: Ask Arun about **paid repair hours** now.
Postpone **replacing my old car** and save the garage wages for rent.
feel: I feel **anxious** because the mine could cut shifts, but I have time to ask Arun about paid garage work.
S2.quote: Two years is not enough time for me to build a cushion from this pay.
fieldNote: Iris names a **specific bridge** into her brother's repair garage.
She knows that bridge may not provide **steady wages**.
The **short timeline** makes a mine cut plausible, while Iris still has a garage lead to explore.

steps.text: Try one paid Saturday each month at Arun's repair garage

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years gives me more time to ask questions than the two-year picture, but it does not make my savings grow by itself. Thinking tasks at the mine would change first, with robots following around 2034.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the newer operators to watch the training notices and keep their safety records clean. I would say a longer warning is useful only if the mine gives us a real path to another position.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would have a chance to move into maintenance support before robots reach the truck work, but I would have to learn on equipment I have not serviced before. I am wary of being the oldest beginner in a classroom, even at 32.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This year I would ask Lena to let me shadow the mechanics during one scheduled service. If that suits me, I would take the mine's entry maintenance course over the next two years instead of paying for outside training.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel worried, but I can see a route that I could test before leaving the cab. I would still keep my current shifts while I find out whether maintenance work is something I can do well.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make you decide the course is worth the effort?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would want a mechanic to show me the work and tell me which certificate the mine recognizes. If the course leads only to unpaid practice, I would not take on debt for it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: In 2032, the first year after thinking AGI arrives, what would you do if the mine changed your planning duties?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would use the maintenance course I had tested to apply for an internal service role. I would stay on the haul truck while waiting for a written offer rather than quit on a promise.

say: I would tell operators to keep their **safety records** clean.
A longer warning needs a **real path** to another role.
think: I could test a move into **maintenance support**.
I will not borrow for training without a **recognized certificate**.
do: Take the mine's **entry course** if it leads to a paid role there.
feel: I feel **anxious**, with a route I can test before leaving the cab.
S3.quote: I would say a longer warning is useful only if the mine gives us a real path to another position.
fieldNote: The five-year lead gives Iris a **trial period**, not comfort.
She wants **recognized training** before committing savings or debt.
A **trial period** lets Iris inspect maintenance work before paying for training.

steps.text: Shadow mine mechanics during one scheduled equipment service
Take the mine's entry maintenance course if recognized

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years sounds less like a warning alarm and more like a chance to see whether the mine is serious. The thinking systems still arrive first in 2036, and I would expect robots to reach truck work around 2039.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would say the extra years should come with proper training, not just another safety poster. I would tell Arun I have time to learn repairs slowly while I still earn mine wages.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be 37 when the thinking system arrives, so I am not near retirement and cannot simply wait it out. A decade gives me room to become useful in maintenance, but I still need the mine to keep paying me while I learn.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would start by asking to join a maintenance shadow shift once each quarter, then set aside overtime for a recognized certificate. In the first year after the 2036 change I would apply for a maintenance slot before robots are expected to reach the trucks.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious rather than panicked because ten years gives me time to build a record. The money worry stays; my savings are still thin today, not in some future decade.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you need from the mine to keep that plan realistic?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would need paid shadow time and to know which certificate counts for an internal transfer. Without those, I would keep my current role and ask Arun about garage work as a second option.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: In 2037, the first year after thinking AGI arrives, what would you do if the mine reorganized your team?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would apply for a maintenance slot before robots were expected to reach the trucks. If no paid training or role existed, I would keep my shift and ask Arun whether his garage had steady work.

say: The extra years should include **proper training**, not posters.
I would tell Arun I can learn repairs while earning **mine wages**.
think: At 37, I would still need a **new role**, not retirement.
The decade helps only if the mine funds **paid learning time**.
do: Apply early for an internal slot before **robots reach the trucks** in 2039.
feel: I feel **anxious**, but ten years gives me time to build a record.
S4.quote: The money worry stays; my savings are still thin today, not in some future decade.
fieldNote: The long timeline lets Iris plan without making her **current insecurity disappear**.
She seeks **paid shadow shifts** and a credential tied to internal hiring.
A **backup job** remains necessary if the mine will not fund learning time.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because I could lose income before building any cushion. Paid repair hours with Arun and a clear mine training route would help me make a move without walking away from wages.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I did not ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: People talk about the equipment, but I think about the next rent payment and whether my skills travel. I do not want sympathy; I want a chance to learn while I am still on payroll.

headlineQuote: People talk about the equipment, but I think about the next rent payment and whether my skills travel.
portrait: Iris Patel is **27** and operates haul trucks at a large mine.
She is highly skilled but earns **lower pay** and has under a month of expenses saved.
**Few nearby jobs** make any roster change a household concern.
She prefers familiar equipment and takes time to trust **new tools**.
She weighs paid maintenance training against the risk of losing **mine wages**.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** could cut income before Iris can build a cushion.
whatWouldHelp: A **paid repair path** and clear mine training timetable would give her options while earning wages.
